analysis.investment_thesis: MedPlus operates in a sector I understand deeply — retail pharmacy — but it fails my non-negotiable financial discipline tests: D/E of 0.65 far exceeds my 0.3 ceiling, promoter holding at 40.29% is below the 55% I require, and a 51x P/E for a 4.75% operating margin business is simply unjustifiable. The business has structural tailwinds, but I will not pay a luxury price for a commodity retailer with mediocre returns on capital.
key_strengths: Revenue CAGR of 15.1% over 9 years is steady and meaningful for a retail chain
FY2025 FCF of INR 482 Cr is a sharp turnaround — finally converting EBITDA of 529 Cr into real cash
Healthcare retail has secular demand growth and is less cyclical than general retail
key_risks: D/E of 0.65 with borrowings rising every year (477→1,193 Cr) — debt-funded store expansion is exactly the model I avoid
ROE of 8.8% is catastrophic for a business trading at 50x earnings — capital is being destroyed in relative terms
E-commerce disruption from 1mg, PharmEasy, and Apollo's online channel threatens the very store-walk-in model that underpins MedPlus's economics
red_flags: Promoter holding at only 40.29% — well below my 55% floor; promoters don't have enough skin in the game
Net profit has been wildly volatile: 9→42→2→95→50→150 Cr — no earnings quality or predictability
Finance costs have risen from 17 Cr (2016) to 103 Cr (2025) as debt compounds — this will suppress PAT margins permanently
P/E of 51x for a business earning 4.75% operating margins leaves zero margin of safety
analysis.detailed_analysis:
I built DMart on owned properties, tight working capital, and zero tolerance for debt — MedPlus is the opposite playbook. Borrowings have compounded at 22% annually for nine years, now sitting at INR 1,193 Cr against equity of INR 1,845 Cr. A D/E of 0.65 is not a pharma-retail norm I can accept; it is a structural fragility that will punish the business in any credit-tight environment. The ROE of 8.8% tells me the market is pricing this as a growth story, but the actual return being generated on shareholders' money is worse than a fixed deposit — I refuse to pay 50x earnings for that outcome.

The one genuinely interesting data point is FY2025 FCF of INR 482 Cr against a historically negative/minimal FCF track record — capex has collapsed from 169 Cr to 59 Cr, suggesting the store-build phase may be maturing. If management sustains that FCF discipline and meaningfully reduces debt over the next two to three years, the thesis could change. But at INR 878 per share and a market cap of 10,544 Cr, the stock is priced for perfection in a low-margin, highly competitive sector facing structural disruption from online pharmacies. I would need the price to halve and the balance sheet to heal before I even open the file again.
